newsitem.title: MEXICO: MEXICAN SOYBEAN TARIFFS SEEN NOT HURTING IMPORTS.
newsitem.headline: MEXICAN SOYBEAN TARIFFS SEEN NOT HURTING IMPORTS.

text.p: Mexico's seasonal soybean tariffs are not seen hurting imports from the United States in coming months despite speculation over whether they will be imposed or not, soybean sources said Thursday.

Local offices of the United Soybean Board and the American Soybean Association (USB-ASA) said they believed the government would impose the seasonal tariffs that are designed to protect domestically grown soybeans.

"There is still no word from the Trade Ministry on whether or not they will allow imports free of tariff this year. The speculation is that they will not allow imports of beans tariff free even if there is such a low 100,000-tonne local crop," USB-ASA said in an update.
This year, a tariff of six percent is scheduled to be enforced on imports of soybeans from nations of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) from October 1 to the end of January.
The NAFTA tariff is essentially one on U.S.-grown beans given Mexico traditionally imports 95 percent of its needs from the United States.

Tariffs of 10 percent for non-NAFTA nations came into effect August 1 and also run through until January 31. This tariff is chiefly directed at Brazil-grown soybeans. The South American nation is traditionally the main competitor to the United States to sell beans to Mexico.
One soybean trader disagreed with the USB-ASA belief and said he expected the government to waive the NATFA tariffs this year just like the last cycle.
"We don't expect them to impose the tariffs. There is enough pressure from crushers saying it would hurt their business and the national harvest is too small anyway," the trader said.

Mexico is currently consuming around 3 million tonnes of soybeans per year. The national crop this year will be between 120,000 and 130,000 tonnes, the trader predicted, adding import demand from the United States was still running high.
USB-ASA agreed that if the government imposed the NAFTA tariffs it would not slow import demand.
"Imports of beans should not be affected much when the tariff goes into effect because demand is still strong and the only viable source is still only the United States," the organizations reported.

USB-ASA said imports of Brazilian beans should be stalled until February because of the tariffs now in place on non-NAFTA nations. Unconfirmed reports from traders indicate that 100,000 tonnes of Brazlian beans entered Mexico in four shiploads during June and July, USB-ASA said.
To July 10, Mexico had imported 2,759,000 tonnes of soybeans from the United States in the Sept 1-Aug 31 farm cycle, according to USB-ASA figures.
Total commitments to purchase soybean to the same date totaled 3,129,000 tonnes, way over the 2.7-million-tonne record imports last cycle, USB-ASA said.
